sources.headline: UK was ‘vehement’ slavery reparations should not be on Commonwealth summit agenda
sources.text: British officials initially insisted that discussions of reparations for slavery should not be on the agenda of the Commonwealth leaders’ summit in Antigua and Barbuda – and even warned that Andy Burnham would not attend the meeting if the subject was formally included, according to a leading Caribbean political figure.Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the reparatory justice movement Repair Campaign, welcomed Britain’s decision to enter structured dialogue on reparations, but said the UK had come “kicking and screaming” to the conversation.Currently, slavery reparations is not on the official agenda of the Commonwealth Heads of Government (Chogm) summit, which begins on Sunday.Trade, climate resilience and finance, sustainable debt, democracy and investment in opportunities for young people are among the stated priorities for the 56-nation bloc spanning Africa, Asia, the Caribbean and the Americas, the Pacific and Europe.“My understanding from informed circles is that Britain was vehement not to have the matter on the agenda. The British officials – and in that regard they were joined by the Canadian officials – were even raising the prospect that if it is on the agenda the prime minister of Britain wouldn’t go,” Gonsalves told the Guardian.Ralph Gonsalves said the British government was coming ‘kicking and screaming to the table of structured dialogue’. Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty Images“They also started to circulate this untruth that India didn’t want it on the agenda, but that was not so at all. India was very supportive at the UN general assembly resolution on March 25th, 2026. So they were spreading this false word about India.”Gonsalves said that the relentless campaign by Caribbean nations, amplified by a growing regional and global reparations movement, has propelled reparatory justice to the heart of the political conversation at the meeting.“Because of what happened at the UN, because of what happened in Africa, what happened in the Caribbean, and all the work which is taking place in Britain itself too, inside of the British parliament, inside of the British Labour party, both in the Commons and the House of Lords, it is an issue which you can’t duck any more,” he said.He added: “The danger of not putting it formally on the agenda is what we see happening now, that everybody who could have foreseen, whether or not it’s formally on the agenda, even the nature of how the discussions take place at the Commonwealth, and certainly in the retreats, it would have been raised.”Irfaan Ali, Guyana’s president, who met King Charles this week in Georgetown, said he was happy ‘the discourse has moved to a position where it should have been’. Photograph: Chris Jackson/PAGonsalves said while the actual structured dialoguewas unlikely to happen at Chogm, it was expected that when the leaders met in their private retreat, the format and details of the dialogue would be discussed.He said: “The British government, they’re coming, kicking and screaming to the table of structured dialogue. But at least they’re coming.”There was no immediate comment from the British government.Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, chair of the Caribbean Community (Caricom) Reparations Commission, had described the meeting as “the Chogm of reparations”, adding that reparatory justice was “the number one item” for the Caribbean as Commonwealth leaders gather in the region.On Friday there was a historic shift in Britain’s position when the British prime minister went further than any of his predecessors by agreeing to structured dialogue and to consider an apology.Though Caribbean governments and campaigners welcomed Burnham’s announcement, made in an op-ed for the Guardian, it was clear that agreeing on forms of reparations was still a priority for the region.Guyana’s president, Irfaan Ali, welcomed Burnham’s statement and called for a Commonwealth subcommittee to work out the details of the dialogue over the next six to 12 months.“I’m happy that finally the discourse has moved to a position where it should have been, where the British government is involved, because that’s the state we are dealing with,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotionAli said the talks should move beyond attempting to put a price on the indignity of slavery and towards addressing its developmental consequences.Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, said of Burnham: ‘Our views differ.’ Photograph: Andrea de Silva/Reuters“How do we identify a system of support where the UK government, with its financial institutions, can sit with countries … and work on a development pathway, identify development gaps, whether in health, education, social services, infrastructure?”Barbados’s prime minister, Mia Mottley, thanked Burnham for “breaking new ground”, while making clear that the two sides remained divided. “On reparations in particular, our views differ, and we will say so plainly and respectfully,” she said.Mottley identified an apology, investment in health and education, tackling systemic poverty and inequality, and fairer debt terms among areas where agreement could be reached.Philip Davis, the prime minister of the Bahamas, Bahamas, stressed the importance of ‘justice, acknowledgment and meaningful address’. Photograph: Chris Jackson/ReutersThe Bahamas prime minister, Philip Davis, said the talks were not simply about “historical remembrance” but “the enduring consequences of slavery and the importance of justice, acknowledgment and meaningful redress”.As the meeting kicks off on Sunday, the 45th anniversary of Antigua and Barbuda’s independence from British colonial rule, King Charles is indicating he will not follow Burnham and offer a full apology, there is still a sense that the reparations fight is far from over.King Charles and Burnham will be greeted with protests as they travel through Antigua’s capital, St John’s, to attend Chogm events.On billboards, placards and T-shirts, in letters and at a candlelight vigil for the thousands of Africans trafficked to Antigua and Barbuda during the transatlantic slave trade, the message from the Caribbean will be clear: there will be calls for an apology and reparations.On Sunday Kemi Badenoch told broadcasters that an apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade would be a “navel-gazing distraction”, describing slavery as an evil “in which people from every continent and region participated”.“I would really like to sit down with my dear sister Kemi and explain to her so that she could get an understanding of what we are talking about,” Gonsalves said, adding that he would like to discuss how reparatory justice could help heal some of the fractures arising from Britain’s multicultural and ethnic tensions.

sources.headline: Burnham ‘open’ to UK slavery apology, but not reparations: Why now?
sources.text: The United Kingdom’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said his country is open to apologising for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade but ruled out reparations, which campaigners have for years called for.Burnham wrote in an opinion article in The Guardian on Friday that Britain would also work on debt restructuring for the poorest countries, marking an historic turn in London’s stance.Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Burnham opens door to formal apology for Britain’s slave tradelist 2 of 4King Charles’s Caribbean tour: Will he discuss slavery reparations?list 3 of 4King Charles on Caribbean tour as calls grow for slavery reparationslist 4 of 4Ghana slavery apology: Why many descendants say words are not enoughend of listThe move comes ahead of a four-day summit starting Sunday of the 50-plus Commonwealth nations formerly colonised by Britain. The UK’s King Charles, who arrived in the Caribbean last week, is hosting the leaders in St John’s, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda.“I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people, and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today,” Burnham wrote, in what amounted to a personal apology.Caribbean nations that have more forcefully demanded reparations in recent years said they expect more from Britain, while opposition Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has criticised Burnham’s move as “navel-gazing”.Here’s what we know:Ankle shackles used in the transatlantic slave trade remain at Fort Prinzenstein in Keta, Ghana, August 8, 2022 [Nita Bhalla/Thomson Reuters Foundation]What was Britain’s role in slavery?Transatlantic slavery lasted between the 16th and 19th centuries and saw some 12 million enslaved Africans torn from their homes and forcibly transported on ships to the Americas with the help of local warlords. Enslaved people were sold on plantations and as domestic workers, and their labour produced goods that built wealth in Europe.Britain and Portugal accounted for about 70 percent of all Africans exported to the Americas, while France, Spain and the Netherlands also traded in significant numbers of enslaved people. Britain alone transported 3.1 million Africans to British colonies in the Caribbean, the Americas and other countries, according to its national archives. Only 2.7 million arrived, as many perished in treacherous sea journeys.British abolitionists began campaigning against slavery in 1787, particularly in cities like Manchester. In 1807, Parliament passed the Slave Trade Act, essentially banning new enslavement. More than three decades later, in 1834, Britain banned slavery in its entirety, although the practice continued for several years.Amid calls for accountability in 2006, then-Prime Minister Tony Blair expressed “deep sorrow” for Britain’s role in the slave trade, but fell short of apologising or speaking about reparations.Why now?Burnham’s apology came during Britain’s Black History Month and as the Commonwealth is meeting in Antigua and Barbuda.In his article, the British prime minister said London wants to keep diplomatic and trade ties with its Commonwealth allies.“In an increasingly divided and dangerous world, our family of nations in the Commonwealth is vital to our interests,” he wrote, adding that Britain “can seize opportunities for trade and economic collaboration”.Britain will allow the most vulnerable countries to repay their debts over a longer period, he added, with former Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown, who spearheaded the UK’s 1991 initiative to reduce debt for poorer countries, leading the charge.Britain’s King Charles III inspects the guard of honour on his arrival at Cheddi Jagan International Airport in Georgetown, Guyana, Thursday, October 29, 2026 [Delano Williams/AP]What is the debate regarding apologies and reparations?Since 2013, the Caribbean Community and Common Market (CARICOM) has called on Western countries involved to acknowledge their role and institute monetary reparations for slavery.In recent years, those calls have grown louder, led by Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley.Ghana, where around 10-15 percent of enslaved people were transferred from, has also played a major role and pushed a historic resolution at the United Nations in March that saw 123 countries vote to declare trafficking of enslaved Africans the gravest crime against humanity. All European nations abstained while the United States, Israel and Argentina voted against the measure.Campaigners argue that there is a legal and moral case for financial payment and debt cancellations for the centuries of damage caused by enslavement. Those damages, they say, are evident in the structural inequalities that continue to plague countries where human capital was stolen from and those in the Caribbean that faced genocides after Europeans arrived.They also point to the loss of lives, the erasure of cultures, the looting of artefacts in the colonial era that followed, and ongoing economic disparities and development challenges that see those nations struggle to access international financial institutions.In June, Mottley announced a 19-point manifesto at a conference in Ghana, as Caribbean and African countries increasingly align to more strongly push their case. It called for a “full and formal apology”, monetary compensation from nations, but also institutions, including corporations and churches. It also called for technology transfer, education and healthcare funding, debt relief and economic development. The plan revised an earlier CARICOM 10-point plan.“We live in a world today where people call out people for everything, for misogyny, for sexual assault, for all kinds of behaviour. But yet we have not found the moral courage to state unanimously across humanity that this grave crime against humanity that persisted for centuries ought to be declared so by all,” Mottley said at the conference.Why are European nations not keen on reparations?European nations, including Britain, argue that those crimes were committed long ago and that, as such, their people should not pay for them. Some also point to the role of local African chiefs who worked with the Europeans to kidnap and enslave people.“I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part,” Burnham wrote in The Guardian.Instead, he said, the UK was “offering a structured dialogue” with those affected and debt restructuring.France recognised slavery as a crime against humanity in 2001. In May, French President Emmanuel Macron said Paris should look into reparations, but did not make clear proposals.In 2022, the Netherlands apologised for its role.The Church of England, whose clergy also owned enslaved people, set up a fund of 100 million British pounds ($134mn) to cater to affected communities and to conduct further research into slavery’s legacies.What are the reactions?In a statement, Saint Lucia’s Prime Minister Philip J Pierre, who currently chairs CARICOM, said the organisation rejects the argument that Britain of today cannot be held responsible for slavery.“Reparatory justice has never been about individual guilt. It is about the responsibility of states and institutions — and that responsibility does not expire with the passing of generations,” he said. Without repair, PM Burnham’s apology was “incomplete”, he added.Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama said he welcomed Burnham’s statement with “caution” and reiterated the need for a formal apology, targeted investments in several sectors, and an international commitment to “dismantle systemic racism and Afrophobia”.Denis O’Brien, founder of the advocacy group The Repair Campaign, also said London “must stop obfuscating and give a full and formal apology now”.The UK’s opposition Conservative Party leader Badenoch kicked against the move entirely in a post on X, and asked whether the descendants of African rulers involved would also be asked for reparations.“There is no reason British taxpayers today should be held financially responsible for things that happened generations before any of us were born,” she said.“Labour are already spending too much on Britain’s welfare state, now is not the time for Andy Burnham to be providing global welfare.”Meanwhile, Bell Ribeiro-Addy, chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) for Afrikan Reparations, which endorses compensation, welcomed Burnham’s steps but said action was still “lacking”.

sources.headline: King acknowledges 'suffering of the past' as Caribbean tour begins
sources.text: King Charles III has begun his tour of the Caribbean by acknowledging the "great suffering of the past" as he faced calls for slavery reparations.Speaking an event in the Bahamas celebrating local youth, the King said the country's culture was "born out of darkness", and it was "only right" to acknowledge historic injustices. His nine-day tour will culminate in the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), where the King has confirmed leaders will discuss the region's legacy of slavery.The visit, his first as monarch, comes in the wake of renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for its role in selling enslaved people for profit.Prior to the trip, Buckingham Palace said the King would not shy away from "colonial legacy" and the impact of the slave trade during his visit but, in line with the UK government position, he will not apologise for Britain's role in the slave trade or offer reparations.Upon his arrival on Tuesday, the King met Governor General Dame Cynthia A. Pratt and its Prime Minister Philip Edward Davis, before speaking with members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force as he inspected a guard of honour.King Charles, wearing sunglasses and a grey suit, was then met with cheers as he arrived for his first engagement at a youth rally at Clifford Park - where he attended independence celebrations for the Bahamas as Prince of Wales in 1973.The young people in the crowd had been given time off school for the event. "It's my first time seeing him in person out of TikTok so he's out there, it's cool," one student told the BBC. A small group of protesters gathered close to the rally shouting "pay us what you owe us" and "return artefacts you've stolen."The group of around a dozen protesters was kept outside the main venue as they called on the King to help change the UK government's position on apologising and offering reparations."He's a man of influence. The Crown still has influence. And if they do not do it then we will become a republic and we will turn our backs on England if you do not show respect to the former colonies," said one protester, Sharon Purcer-Cooper. During his speech in Nassau, the King acknowledged his 50-year-long commitment to fighting climate change and highlighted the challenges faced by low-lying Caribbean islands, saying that "our world cries out for healing".He went on to call on young people at the rally to "take up the sacred task to play your part" as "in years to come, this will be surely be the measure of every person - how they answered the call to care for planet earth - the source of our life, our prosperity and our security".The King resumes engagements in the Bahamas on Wednesday, where he will hear how vulnerable the low lying islands of the Caribbean are to climate change. He will also learn more about the Bahamian tradition of Junkanoo - a cultural festival and street parade.Buckingham Palace said opportunities for the King to reflect on the legacy of the slave trade will be built into the schedule of his nine-day tour of three Caribbean countries with visits planned to memorials and other places of reflection and remembrance.A spokesperson for the palace told the BBC that the King's programme on the tour "will primarily focus on shining a light on the many modern partnerships and opportunities for the future", specifically those which are "having a transformative effect on the region". For the King, the spokesperson added, the "tour is both a new journey but also the continuance of a lifelong one, in which he has sought to engage, understand and educate about the most shameful aspects of our past".Those themes will be reflected by the King through the nine-day visit, the palace said.The visit has been planned alongside the governments of the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda with an emphasis on honouring the past but also looking forward to the ambition and possibility for future generations.The King will move to Guyana later this week where his engagements will focus on the environment and biodiversity. He will then visit Antigua and Barbuda, where he will be joined by Queen Camilla, for the CHOGM and his keynote speech as leader of the Commonwealth.The biennial summit will bring together leaders of 56 Commonwealth countries to address shared challenges and advance cooperation.

King Charles confronts calls for slavery apology during Caribbean tour

King Charles III began a Caribbean tour in the Bahamas on Tuesday, acknowledging “the great suffering of the past” amid calls for an apology over slavery. The 77-year-old monarch, who is undergoing cancer treatment, will also visit Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda, highlighting climate threats and attending a Commonwealth summit with Queen Camilla.

Issued on: 28/10/2026 - 00:14
Modified: 28/10/2026 - 07:51

  4 min
Reading time
Share
By:
FRANCE 24
Britain's King Charles III will walk a diplomatic tightrope when he visits Caribbean nations this week amid a growing clamour for an apology for the slave trade and reparations. © Aaron Chown, AFP

King Charles III began a Caribbean tour in the Bahamas Tuesday where he acknowledged "the great suffering of the past" in the face of pressure to apologise for the slave trade.

The 77-year-old king, who is receiving treatment for an undisclosed form of cancer, will also highlight climate threats facing low-lying islands during his visit to three countries in nine days.

He will first make solo visits to the Bahamas and Guyana, before being joined by his wife, Queen Camilla, for the final leg in Antigua and Barbuda, where he will address a Commonwealth heads of government (CHOGM) summit.

"We know that some of what is best in Bahamian culture today, the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright, was born out of darkness," he said at a youth rally. 

"It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present and build new opportunities for the future."

Read moreGhana pushes for concrete slavery reparations

He said leaders of "affected" Commonwealth nations would be discussing the issue in Antigua and Barbuda next week where the issue of reparations for slavery will be on the table according to Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey.

Several of the former colonies have demanded the king take a new step toward making amends for colonisation and the transatlantic slave trade, from which his ancestors profited for centuries.

As he arrived at the rally held at the historic site where The Bahamas officially gained its independence in 1973, protesters gathered to wave placards reading "pay what you owe us."

Last month Jamaica – where Charles remains head of state – filed a petition in an appeals court in London "to advance Jamaica's push for reparations for the African ancestors who suffered under hundreds of years of enslavement."

Charles has previously called slavery the "darkest days" of British history, and will address colonial issues at each stage of the trip.

Few in royal circles will have forgotten a turbulent 2022 trip to Jamaica by Prince William, when he and Princess Catherine were met with anti-monarchy protests and calls for reparations.

Read moreFrench slavery law repealed: 'Now we can start talking about reparations,' historian says

Guyana's President Irfaan Ali, who is to meet with Charles during the visit, told ITV News the king's recognition of the "darkest days" was just the "first step."

"Now, moving to the apology is the next step," said Ali, demanding accountability from the former empire which he said "exploited the region," "destroyed lives" and "created under development."

Modern monarchs have to various degrees expressed remorse for Britain's central role in chattel slavery, but none has yet formally apologised. The debt-laden UK government has balked at the idea of financial compensation.

Botchwey told Sky News ahead of the government meeting from November 1 to 4, that it "wouldn't hurt" for the king to apologise.

Botchwey also said the "time has come" to discuss reparations, in the form of financial payments or otherwise.

Read moreMacron backs symbolic repeal of France's slavery laws, warns against 'false promises' on reparations

Climate resilience 

Buckingham Palace has insisted the tour is an opportunity for the king to look forward, meet young people and discuss pressing issues like climate change.

In his Bahamas speech, Charles also highlighted the particular threat facing low-lying islands face from climate change.

"In an island nation where 90 percent of the land sits below two meters (six foot, six inches). There is perhaps nowhere better than the Bahamas to understand the reality of climate change that threatens so many communities across the Commonwealth," he said. "Our world cries out for healing."

According to Botchwey, the Commonwealth, which includes 56 member countries with the king at its helm, is an important anchor in a "world that is almost spinning out of control".

"This CHOGM is going to be one like never before," the secretary-general told AFP in an interview, with the meeting in St John's set to focus on investment and trade opportunities for member countries.

Charles, who has long championed environmental causes, will meet organisations working in the field, including a coral restoration project in Antigua and Barbuda and rainforest conservation in Guyana.

"Many of these countries that are affected by climate are not polluters, and yet they feel the brunt of the effects of climate," said Botchwey, adding that the CHOGM summit will also touch upon climate resilience schemes.

While she refused to elaborate on whether the UK government and royals should pursue slavery reparations, she said the issue would be on the table in St John's.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Published: 7:36am, 28 Oct 2026Updated: 12:13pm, 28 Oct 2026

Britain’s King Charles arrived in the Bahamas on Tuesday as part of a nine-day trip to the Caribbean, where he faces calls for an apology and slavery reparations.

It is his first official visit to the Bahamas as king, with the archipelago’s government closing all public schools on the island of New Providence to welcome him.

The Bahamian police and armed forces strode out to greet Charles in lockstep, some wearing pith helmets. Charles stepped out in a light grey suit and donned sunglasses as he greeted Governor-General Dame Cynthia A. Pratt and Prime Minister Philip Davis.

Charles then travelled to Clifford Park, which he last officially visited as Prince of Wales in 1973 to grant the Bahamas independence after 300 years of British rule.

Members of the Bahamas’ Rastafarian community and others lined a road near Clifford Park in protest, demanding reparations. “Pay us what you owe us!” one woman cried out. “I stand in memory of the horrors and the atrocities committed against black people.”

Meanwhile, a cheering crowd awaited Charles as he arrived at the park, with dozens of young students waving small Bahamian flags ahead of a cultural event that included children singing and playing music.

Britain’s King Charles is received by Dame Cynthia Pratt, Governor-General of The Bahamas, in Nassau on Tuesday. Photo: Reuters

“We know that some of what is best in Bahamian culture today, the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright, was born out of darkness,” Charles said in his first public remarks since arriving in the Bahamas.

“It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present.”

Jamaica recently took its case for reparations to Charles, and the case has since been referred to the UK’s highest court of appeal for the Caribbean island. The British government, however, has consistently rejected demands for either an apology or reparations.

While in the Bahamas, Charles also is expected to visit a nature site and meet with the Royal Bahamas Defence Force as well as government officials and civil society leaders.

Some in the Bahamas hope his visit will draw attention to an ongoing environmental struggle on an island that forms part of the Exuma cays.

Eric Carey, former executive director of the Bahamas National Trust, said the Save Exuma Alliance is fighting a development on Sampson Cay that he called “ill-advised” and “out of scale”. He noted that the development calls for a “massive” sea wall and the dredging of sea grass and coral reefs.

“This is not a position of antidevelopment; our country is a tourism-based economy,” Carey said in a phone interview. “Our point is that there are larger islands where larger scale developments could be more effectively and efficiently constructed.”

Britain’s King Charles and Philip Davis, Prime Minister of The Bahamas, applaud as they attend a youth rally in Clifford Park in Nassau on Tuesday. Photo: Reuters

The case is currently in the hands of the Bahamas Supreme Court, but Carey said he hopes Charles will raise awareness about the issue.

“King Charles has a long history of defending the environment, talking about climate change,” Carey said. “He’s visiting … one of the most vulnerable regions in the world.”

During his speech at Clifford Park, Charles acknowledged the climate challenges that the Bahamas and other nations face.

“We cannot escape the fact that the journey ahead contains some treacherous shoals, in particular in an island nation where 90 per cent of the land sits below two metres,” Charles said.

“There is perhaps nowhere better than the Bahamas to understand the reality of climate change.”

Charles is scheduled to spend three days in the Bahamas and then fly to the South American country of Guyana on October 29, where he will spend two days in the former British colony whose president has said he wants an apology.

Charles is then scheduled to fly to Antigua and Barbuda on October 30 for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, where Queen Camilla will join him.

Talks are expected to focus on climate, trade and development, but some Caribbean leaders have said slavery reparations should dominate conversations.

the table, according to Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey.Several of the former colonies have demanded the King take a new step towards making amends for colonisation and the transatlantic slave trade, from which his ancestors profited for centuries.As he arrived at the rally held at the historic site where the Bahamas officially gained its independence in 1973, protesters gathered to wave placards reading “pay what you owe us”.In September, Jamaica – where Charles remains head of state – filed a petition in an appeals court in London “to advance Jamaica’s push for reparations for the African ancestors who suffered under hundreds of years of enslavement”.Charles has previously called slavery the “darkest days” of British history, and will address colonial issues at each stage of the trip.Few in royal circles will have forgotten a turbulent 2022 trip to Jamaica by Prince William, when he and Princess Catherine were met with anti-monarchy protests and calls for reparations.Guyana’s President Irfaan Ali, who is to meet Charles during the visit, told ITV News the King’s recognition of the “darkest days” was just the first step.“Now, moving to the apology is the next step,” said Ali, demanding accountability from the former empire which he said “exploited the region”, “destroyed lives” and “created under-development”.Modern monarchs have in various degrees expressed remorse for Britain’s central role in chattel slavery, but none has yet formally apologised.The debt-laden British government has baulked at the idea of financial compensation.Botchwey told Sky News ahead of the government meeting from Nov 1 to Nov 4, that it “wouldn’t hurt” for the King to apologise.Botchwey also said the “time has come” to discuss reparations, in the form of financial payments or otherwise.Climate resilienceBuckingham Palace has insisted the tour is an opportunity for the King to look forward, meet young people and discuss pressing issues like climate change.In his Bahamas speech, Charles also highlighted the particular threat low-lying islands face from climate change.“In an island nation where 90% of the land sits below 2m, there is perhaps nowhere better than the Bahamas to understand the reality of climate change that threatens so many communities across the Commonwealth,” he said.“Our world cries out for healing.”According to Botchwey, the Commonwealth, which includes 56 member countries with the King at its helm, is an important anchor in a “world that is almost spinning out of control”.“This CHOGM is going to be one like never before,” the secretary-general told AFP in an interview, with the meeting in St John’s set to focus on investment and trade opportunities for member countries.Charles, who has long championed environmental causes, will meet organisations working in the field, including a coral restoration project in Antigua and Barbuda, and rainforest conservation in Guyana.“Many of these countries that are affected by climate are not polluters, and yet they feel the brunt of the effects of climate,” said Botchwey, adding that the CHOGM summit will also touch upon climate resilience schemes.While she refused to elaborate on whether the British government and royals should pursue slavery reparations, she said the issue would be on the table in St John’s.
